title: Hummus
subtitle: smooth chickpea dip with tahini and lemon
excerpt: A smooth, pale hummus made from blended chickpeas, tahini, lemon, and garlic. The key is to peel the chickpeas and blend for long enough. It is better than anything from a shop.
sourceNotes: Hummus is eaten across the Middle East and North Africa and has been made for hundreds of years. Its exact origin is contested between Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, and other countries in the region.

recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the batch. Stores in the fridge for 4 to 5 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 4 days ahead. Drizzle with olive oil before serving.

content.text: Peel the chickpeas before blending. Pinch each one between your thumb and finger -- the skin slips off. This step takes a few minutes but results in a much smoother, paler hummus. Blend for at least 3 minutes.

items.prepNote: 2 x 400g tins, drained -- reserve the liquid

content.text: Drain the chickpeas. Peel as many as you can by pinching off the skins.
Put the chickpeas, garlic, tahini (or yoghurt), lemon juice, salt, and cumin into a food processor.
Blend for 3 to 4 minutes, adding the reserved chickpea liquid a tablespoon at a time until the hummus is very smooth and pale.
Taste and adjust the lemon, salt, and garlic. It should be bright, nutty, and savoury.
Spread into a shallow bowl. Drizzle with olive oil and dust with smoked paprika to serve.

items.cause: Not blended long enough or skins not removed
items.fix: Blend for at least 4 minutes. Peel as many chickpeas as possible before blending. Adding ice water while blending also helps.
Add the reserved chickpea liquid a tablespoon at a time while the processor is running.

items.cause: Not enough salt, lemon, or garlic
items.fix: Taste after blending and adjust all three. Hummus needs generous salt and lemon.

content.text: Hummus is eaten daily across Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Syria, and beyond. Its origin is disputed with considerable passion among the nations of the Levant. What is clear is that it has been eaten in the Middle East for centuries and is now one of the most widely eaten foods in the world. The debate about who invented it is unlikely to be settled.
